claim: Fibroblasts lacking either talin or kindlin failed to activate β1 integrins.
source: Here we report that fibroblasts lacking either talin or kindlin failed to activate β1 integrins, adhere to fibronectin (FN) or maintain their integrins in a high affinity conformation induced by Mn2+.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from flow cytometry showing 9EG7 epitope exposure and AFM-based single cell force spectroscopy measurements.

claim: Fibroblasts lacking either talin or kindlin failed to adhere to fibronectin (FN).
source: Here we report that fibroblasts lacking either talin or kindlin failed to activate β1 integrins, adhere to fibronectin (FN) or maintain their integrins in a high affinity conformation induced by Mn2+.
evidence: Supported by plate and wash adhesion assays showing TlnKo and KindKo cells did not adhere to FN.

claim: Fibroblasts lacking either talin or kindlin failed to maintain their integrins in a high affinity conformation induced by Mn2+.
source: Here we report that fibroblasts lacking either talin or kindlin failed to activate β1 integrins, adhere to fibronectin (FN) or maintain their integrins in a high affinity conformation induced by Mn2+.
evidence: Supported by AFM-based single cell force spectroscopy and 9EG7 antibody binding measurements showing reduced integrin activation in Mn2+-treated TlnKo and KindKo cells.

claim: Mn2+ enabled talin- but not kindlin-deficient cells to initiate spreading on FN.
source: Despite compromised integrin activation and adhesion, Mn2+ enabled talin- but not kindlin-deficient cells to initiate spreading on FN.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing 37% of TlnKo cells formed circumferential lamellipodia with Mn2+ treatment, while only 7% of KindKo cells did so.

claim: Kindlin induces isotropic spreading by directly binding paxillin.
source: This isotropic spreading was induced by the ability of kindlin to directly bind paxillin, which in turn bound focal adhesion kinase (FAK) resulting in FAK activation and the formation of lamellipodia.
evidence: Supported by yeast-two-hybrid screening, immunoprecipitation experiments, and recombinant protein pull-down assays demonstrating direct interaction between kindlin-2 and paxillin.

claim: Paxillin bound focal adhesion kinase (FAK) resulting in FAK activation and the formation of lamellipodia.
source: This isotropic spreading was induced by the ability of kindlin to directly bind paxillin, which in turn bound focal adhesion kinase (FAK) resulting in FAK activation and the formation of lamellipodia.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing pY397-FAK phosphorylation in TlnKo cells but not KindKo cells, and immunofluorescence showing FAK localization.

claim: Talin and kindlin cooperatively activate integrins leading to FN binding and adhesion.
source: Our findings show that talin and kindlin cooperatively activate integrins leading to FN binding and adhesion, and that kindlin subsequently assembles an essential signaling node at newly formed adhesion sites in a talin-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by 9EG7 epitope exposure measurements, AFM-based adhesion force measurements, and adhesion assays showing both proteins are required for integrin activation.

claim: Kindlin assembles an essential signaling node at newly formed adhesion sites in a talin-independent manner.
source: Our findings show that talin and kindlin cooperatively activate integrins leading to FN binding and adhesion, and that kindlin subsequently assembles an essential signaling node at newly formed adhesion sites in a talin-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence showing paxillin recruitment to nascent adhesions in TlnKo cells expressing kindlin-2, and western blot data showing FAK activation.

claim: Integrins are heterodimeric transmembrane receptors that mediate cell adhesion to the extracellular matrix (ECM) and to other cells.
source: Integrins are heterodimeric transmembrane receptors that mediate cell adhesion to the extracellular matrix (ECM) and to other cells (Hynes, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature (Hynes, 2002).

claim: Integrin-mediated adhesion results in the assembly of a large molecular network that induces various signaling pathways, resulting in cell migration, proliferation, survival and differentiation.
source: The consequence of integrin-mediated adhesion is the assembly of a large molecular network that induces various signaling pathways, resulting in cell migration, proliferation, survival and differentiation (Winograd-Katz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature (Winograd-Katz et al., 2014).

claim: The affinity switch of integrins proceeds from a bent and clasped low affinity conformation to an extended and unclasped high affinity conformation with an open ligand-binding pocket.
source: The affinity switch proceeds from a bent and clasped low affinity conformation to an extended and unclasped high affinity conformation with an open ligand-binding pocket (Askari et al., 2010; Springer and Dustin, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Askari et al., 2010; Springer and Dustin, 2012).

claim: The change in integrin affinity is believed to be induced through the binding of talin and kindlin to the β integrin cytoplasmic domain.
source: This change in affinity is believed to be induced through the binding of talin and kindlin to the β integrin cytoplasmic domain (Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010) and divalent cations to distinct sites close to the ligand-binding pocket (Gailit and Ruoslahti, 1988; Mould et al., 1995; Xia and Springer, 2014; Mould et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010).

claim: Divalent cations induce changes in integrin affinity by binding to distinct sites close to the ligand-binding pocket.
source: This change in affinity is believed to be induced through the binding of talin and kindlin to the β integrin cytoplasmic domain (Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010) and divalent cations to distinct sites close to the ligand-binding pocket (Gailit and Ruoslahti, 1988; Mould et al., 1995; Xia and Springer, 2014; Mould et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Gailit and Ruoslahti, 1988; Mould et al., 1995; Xia and Springer, 2014; Mould et al., 2003).

claim: The stabilisation of integrin–ligand complexes is mediated by integrin clustering and catch bond formation between integrin and bound ligand.
source: The stabilisation of integrin–ligand complexes is mediated by integrin clustering and catch bond formation between integrin and bound ligand.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on integrin clustering and catch bonds in subsequent sentences.

claim: The stabilizing effect of clustered integrins is achieved by the ability of dissociated integrin–ligand complexes to rebind before they leave the adhesion site.
source: The stabilizing effect of clustered integrins is achieved by the ability of dissociated integrin–ligand complexes to rebind before they leave the adhesion site (van Kooyk and Figdor, 2000; Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009), while catch bonds are receptor–ligand bonds whose lifetime increases with mechanical force (Kong et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (van Kooyk and Figdor, 2000; Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009).

claim: Catch bonds are receptor–ligand bonds whose lifetime increases with mechanical force.
source: The stabilizing effect of clustered integrins is achieved by the ability of dissociated integrin–ligand complexes to rebind before they leave the adhesion site (van Kooyk and Figdor, 2000; Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009), while catch bonds are receptor–ligand bonds whose lifetime increases with mechanical force (Kong et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Kong et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2013).

claim: Integrin clustering and catch bonds extend the duration and increase the strength of integrin-mediated adhesion and signaling.
source: Both mechanisms extend the duration and increase the strength of integrin-mediated adhesion and signaling (also called outside-in signaling) (Koo et al., 2002; van Kooyk and Figdor, 2000; Maheshwari et al., 2000; Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009; Coussen et al., 2002), and depend on the association of integrins with the actin cytoskeleton via talin (Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009; Friedland et al., 2009), and probably kindlin (Ye et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Koo et al., 2002; van Kooyk and Figdor, 2000; Maheshwari et al., 2000; Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009; Coussen et al., 2002).

claim: Integrin clustering and catch bonds depend on the association of integrins with the actin cytoskeleton via talin.
source: Both mechanisms extend the duration and increase the strength of integrin-mediated adhesion and signaling (also called outside-in signaling) (Koo et al., 2002; van Kooyk and Figdor, 2000; Maheshwari et al., 2000; Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009; Coussen et al., 2002), and depend on the association of integrins with the actin cytoskeleton via talin (Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009; Friedland et al., 2009), and probably kindlin (Ye et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009; Friedland et al., 2009).

claim: Integrin clustering and catch bonds probably depend on the association of integrins with the actin cytoskeleton via kindlin.
source: Both mechanisms extend the duration and increase the strength of integrin-mediated adhesion and signaling (also called outside-in signaling) (Koo et al., 2002; van Kooyk and Figdor, 2000; Maheshwari et al., 2000; Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009; Coussen et al., 2002), and depend on the association of integrins with the actin cytoskeleton via talin (Roca-Cusachs et al., 2009; Friedland et al., 2009), and probably kindlin (Ye et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature (Ye et al., 2013) with speculative language 'probably'.

claim: The talin family consists of two isoforms (talin-1 and -2).
source: The talin family consists of two (talin-1 and -2) and the kindlin family of three isoforms (kindlin-1-3), which show tissue-specific expression patterns (Calderwood et al., 2013; Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Calderwood et al., 2013; Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010).

claim: The kindlin family consists of three isoforms (kindlin-1-3).
source: The talin family consists of two (talin-1 and -2) and the kindlin family of three isoforms (kindlin-1-3), which show tissue-specific expression patterns (Calderwood et al., 2013; Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Calderwood et al., 2013; Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010).

claim: Talin and kindlin show tissue-specific expression patterns.
source: The talin family consists of two (talin-1 and -2) and the kindlin family of three isoforms (kindlin-1-3), which show tissue-specific expression patterns (Calderwood et al., 2013; Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Calderwood et al., 2013; Moser et al., 2009; Shattil et al., 2010).

claim: Agonist-induced signaling pathways activate talin-1 and kindlin-3, which cooperate to induce integrin activation in platelets and leukocytes.
source: The prevailing view is that agonist-induced signaling pathways activate talin-1 and the hematopoietic cell-specific kindlin-3, which cooperate to induce integrin activation (Moser et al., 2008; Han et al., 2006) and clustering (Cluzel et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Moser et al., 2008; Han et al., 2006).

claim: Talin-1 and kindlin-3 cooperate to induce integrin clustering in platelets and leukocytes.
source: The prevailing view is that agonist-induced signaling pathways activate talin-1 and the hematopoietic cell-specific kindlin-3, which cooperate to induce integrin activation (Moser et al., 2008; Han et al., 2006) and clustering (Cluzel et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Cluzel et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2013).

claim: Talin and kindlin are required for integrin activation in epithelial cells.
source: While there are reports showing that talin and kindlin are required for integrin activation in epithelial cells (Montanez et al., 2008; Margadant et al., 2012), it was also shown that in myoblasts and mammary epithelial cells activation of β1 integrins, adhesion and spreading on multiple ECM substrates can proceed in the absence of talin (Conti et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature (Montanez et al., 2008; Margadant et al., 2012).

claim: In myoblasts and mammary epithelial cells activation of β1 integrins, adhesion and spreading on multiple ECM substrates can proceed in the absence of talin.
source: While there are reports showing that talin and kindlin are required for integrin activation in epithelial cells (Montanez et al., 2008; Margadant et al., 2012), it was also shown that in myoblasts and mammary epithelial cells activation of β1 integrins, adhesion and spreading on multiple ECM substrates can proceed in the absence of talin (Conti et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature (Conti et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: FAK-deficient fibroblasts develop small, nascent adhesions (NAs) at the edge of membrane protrusions without visible talin.
source: Likewise, it was reported that focal adhesion kinase (FAK)-deficient fibroblasts develop small, nascent adhesions (NAs) at the edge of membrane protrusions without visible talin and that integrins carrying a mutation in the talin-binding site can still nucleate and stabilize NAs (Lawson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature (Lawson et al., 2012).

claim: Integrins carrying a mutation in the talin-binding site can still nucleate and stabilize NAs.
source: Likewise, it was reported that focal adhesion kinase (FAK)-deficient fibroblasts develop small, nascent adhesions (NAs) at the edge of membrane protrusions without visible talin and that integrins carrying a mutation in the talin-binding site can still nucleate and stabilize NAs (Lawson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature (Lawson et al., 2012).

claim: Fibroblasts lacking talin-1 and -2 adhere to fibronectin and initiate isotropic spreading.
source: Also fibroblasts lacking talin-1 and -2 were shown to adhere to fibronectin (FN) and initiate isotropic spreading (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature (Zhang et al., 2008).

claim: Overexpression of kindlin-2 in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells inhibits talin head-induced α5β1 integrin activation.
source: Another intriguing study demonstrated that overexpression of kindlin-2 in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells inhibits rather than promotes talin head-induced α5β1 integrin activation (Harburger et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature (Harburger et al., 2009).

claim: Loss of talin-1 or kindlin-2 expression in fibroblasts was compensated by talin-2 or the de novo expression of kindlin-1, respectively.
source: Loss of talin-1 or kindlin-2 expression in fibroblasts was compensated by talin-2 or the de novo expression of kindlin-1, respectively, allowing adhesion and spreading, although to a lesser extent compared with control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data and immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Cre-mediated deletion of the floxed Tln1 or floxed Fermt1/2 genes resulted in cell rounding, weak adhesion of a few cells, and reduced cell proliferation.
source: Cre-mediated deletion of the floxed Tln1 or floxed Fermt1/2 genes was efficient (Figure 1B) and resulted in cell rounding, weak adhesion of a few cells, and reduced cell proliferation despite the immortalisation with the oncogenic large T antigen (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by bright field images in Figure 1C and cell proliferation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: TlnKo and KindKo cells did not adhere to FN, laminin-111 (LN), type I collagen (COL) and vitronectin (VN).
source: To define the adhesion defect, we performed plate and wash assays for 30 min on defined substrates and found that neither TlnKo nor KindKo cells adhered to FN, laminin-111 (LN), type I collagen (COL) and vitronectin (VN) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Treatment with Mn2+ induced partial adhesion of TlnKo and KindKo cells to FN.
source: Treatment with Mn2+ induced partial adhesion of TlnKo and KindKo cells to FN, while partial adhesion to LN and VN was only induced in TlnKo cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Partial adhesion to LN and VN was only induced in TlnKo cells by Mn2+ treatment.
source: Treatment with Mn2+ induced partial adhesion of TlnKo and KindKo cells to FN, while partial adhesion to LN and VN was only induced in TlnKo cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mn2+-induced adhesion of TlnKo and KindKo cells to FN was significantly lower 2.5 min after plating compared with control cells.
source: Time course experiments revealed that Mn2+-induced adhesion of TlnKo and KindKo cells to FN was already significantly lower 2.5 min after plating and remained significantly lower compared with control cells (Figure 1E), suggesting that talin and kindlin cooperate to initiate and maintain normal Mn2+-induced adhesion to FN.
evidence: Supported by time course adhesion data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Talin and kindlin cooperate to initiate and maintain normal Mn2+-induced adhesion to FN.
source: Time course experiments revealed that Mn2+-induced adhesion of TlnKo and KindKo cells to FN was already significantly lower 2.5 min after plating and remained significantly lower compared with control cells (Figure 1E), suggesting that talin and kindlin cooperate to initiate and maintain normal Mn2+-induced adhesion to FN.
evidence: Inferred from time course adhesion data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The levels of β1 and β3 integrins were significantly reduced in KindKo cells.
source: We quantified integrin surface levels by flow cytometry and found that the levels of β1 and β3 were significantly reduced in KindKo and unaffected in TlnKo cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The levels of β1 and β3 integrins were unaffected in TlnKo cells.
source: We quantified integrin surface levels by flow cytometry and found that the levels of β1 and β3 were significantly reduced in KindKo and unaffected in TlnKo cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The β5 integrin levels were similarly up-regulated in KindKo and TlnKo cells.
source: The β5 levels were similarly up-regulated in KindKo and TlnKo cells, and the α5 and αv integrin levels were slightly reduced but not significantly different between TlnKo and KindKo cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The α5 and αv integrin levels were slightly reduced but not significantly different between TlnKo and KindKo cells.
source: The β5 levels were similarly up-regulated in KindKo and TlnKo cells, and the α5 and αv integrin levels were slightly reduced but not significantly different between TlnKo and KindKo cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TlnCtr and KindCtr cells bound 9EG7 antibodies, while TlnKo and KindKo cells lacked 9EG7 binding in the absence of Mn2+.
source: These measurements revealed that TlnCtr and KindCtr cells bound 9EG7 antibodies, while TlnKo and KindKo cells lacked 9EG7 binding in the absence of Mn2+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Mn2+ treatment significantly increased 9EG7 binding by TlnCtr and KindCtr cells.
source: Mn2+ treatment significantly increased 9EG7 binding by TlnCtr and KindCtr cells, which was further elevated in the presence of FN-Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) ligand known to stabilize the high affinity state of integrins (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Mn2+-treated TlnKo and KindKo cells bound significantly less 9EG7 antibodies than control cells.
source: Mn2+-treated TlnKo and KindKo cells bound significantly less 9EG7 antibodies than control cells, which marginally increased with FN-RGD (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Both talin and kindlin are required for β1 integrin activation and to stabilize Mn2+-induced unbending/unclasping of α5β1 integrins.
source: These findings confirm that both, talin and kindlin are required for β1 integrin activation and to stabilize Mn2+-induced unbending/unclasping of α5β1 integrins.
evidence: Inferred from 9EG7 binding data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In the absence of Mn2+ TlnCtr and KindCtr cells developed significant adhesion to FN-RGD within 5 s contact time.
source: In the absence of Mn2+ TlnCtr and KindCtr cells developed significant adhesion to FN-RGD within 5 s contact time. After a contact time of 20 s around 2 nN force was required to disrupt adhesion to FN-RGD, and after 50 and 120 s, respectively, 3 and 6 nN were required (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by AFM-based single cell force spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TlnKo and KindKo cells failed to develop measurable adhesions to FN-RGD after contact times of 5, 20, 50 and 120 s in the absence of Mn2+.
source: TlnKo and KindKo cells failed to develop measurable adhesions to FN-RGD after contact times of 5, 20, 50 and 120 s (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by AFM-based single cell force spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment with Mn2+ induced a slight and similar increase of force required to disrupt adhesion of control, TlnKo and KindKo cells to FN-RGD after 5 s contact time.
source: Treatment with Mn2+ induced a slight and similar increase of force required to disrupt adhesion of control, TlnKo and KindKo cells to FN-RGD after 5 s contact time (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by AFM-based single cell force spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The adhesion force increased concomitantly with longer contact times in TlnCtr, KindCtr and TlnKo cells in the presence of Mn2+.
source: However, with increasing contact times, the AFM profiles of TlnKo and KindKo cells differ in the presence of Mn2+. While the adhesion force increased concomitantly with longer contact times in TlnCtr, KindCtr and TlnKo cells, adhesion forces of KindKo cells plateaued after 50 s and showed no further increase towards 120 s contact time.
evidence: Supported by AFM-based single cell force spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adhesion forces of KindKo cells plateaued after 50 s and showed no further increase towards 120 s contact time in the presence of Mn2+.
source: However, with increasing contact times, the AFM profiles of TlnKo and KindKo cells differ in the presence of Mn2+. While the adhesion force increased concomitantly with longer contact times in TlnCtr, KindCtr and TlnKo cells, adhesion forces of KindKo cells plateaued after 50 s and showed no further increase towards 120 s contact time.
evidence: Supported by AFM-based single cell force spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Kindlin stabilizes integrin–ligand complexes with time, by inducing integrin clustering and/or by modulating the off-rate of integrin ligand bonds.
source: The latter finding suggests that kindlin stabilizes integrin–ligand complexes with time, by inducing integrin clustering and/or by modulating the off-rate of integrin ligand bonds, for example, through associating with the integrin-linked kinase (ILK)-Pinch-Parvin (IPP) complex that links kindlin to the F-actin cytoskeleton (Cluzel et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2013; Montanez et al., 2008; Fukuda et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from AFM data and supported by citations to literature (Cluzel et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2013; Montanez et al., 2008; Fukuda et al., 2014).

claim: Neither TlnKo nor KindKo cells were able to assemble FN fibrils.
source: We next tested whether their impaired integrin function affects the assembly of FN into fibrils, which requires association of active α5β1 integrin with the actin cytoskeleton (Pankov et al., 2000), and whether re-expression of talin and kindlin reverts the defects of TlnKo and KindKo cells. While neither TlnKo nor KindKo cells were able to assemble FN fibrils, re-expression of full-length Venus-tagged talin-1 (Tln1V) in TlnKo or GFP-tagged kindlin-2 (K2GFP) in KindKo cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) rescued FN fibril assembly and adhesion to FN (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images showing FN staining in Figure 2D.

claim: Re-expression of full-length Venus-tagged talin-1 (Tln1V) in TlnKo cells rescued FN fibril assembly and adhesion to FN.
source: While neither TlnKo nor KindKo cells were able to assemble FN fibrils, re-expression of full-length Venus-tagged talin-1 (Tln1V) in TlnKo or GFP-tagged kindlin-2 (K2GFP) in KindKo cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) rescued FN fibril assembly and adhesion to FN (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Re-expression of GFP-tagged kindlin-2 (K2GFP) in KindKo cells rescued FN fibril assembly and adhesion to FN.
source: While neither TlnKo nor KindKo cells were able to assemble FN fibrils, re-expression of full-length Venus-tagged talin-1 (Tln1V) in TlnKo or GFP-tagged kindlin-2 (K2GFP) in KindKo cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) rescued FN fibril assembly and adhesion to FN (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Overexpression of the talin-1 head (THD) or K2GFP in TlnKo cells failed to rescue adhesion to FN or 9EG7 binding.
source: Furthermore, neither overexpression of the talin-1 head (THD) nor K2GFP in TlnKo cells, nor Tln1V or THD in KindKo cells rescued adhesion to FN or 9EG7 binding (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by adhesion assay data in Figure 2E and flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Overexpression of Tln1V or THD in KindKo cells failed to rescue adhesion to FN or 9EG7 binding.
source: Furthermore, neither overexpression of the talin-1 head (THD) nor K2GFP in TlnKo cells, nor Tln1V or THD in KindKo cells rescued adhesion to FN or 9EG7 binding (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by adhesion assay data in Figure 2E and flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Both talin and kindlin are required for ligand-induced stabilisation of integrin-ligand complexes.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that both talin and kindlin are required (1) for ligand-induced stabilisation of integrin-ligand complexes, (2) to stabilize Mn2+-activated α5β1 integrins, and (3) to induce integrin-mediated FN fibril formation.
evidence: Inferred from AFM data, 9EG7 binding data, and FN fibril assembly data.

claim: Both talin and kindlin are required to stabilize Mn2+-activated α5β1 integrins.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that both talin and kindlin are required (1) for ligand-induced stabilisation of integrin-ligand complexes, (2) to stabilize Mn2+-activated α5β1 integrins, and (3) to induce integrin-mediated FN fibril formation.
evidence: Inferred from AFM data, 9EG7 binding data, and FN fibril assembly data.

claim: Both talin and kindlin are required to induce integrin-mediated FN fibril formation.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that both talin and kindlin are required (1) for ligand-induced stabilisation of integrin-ligand complexes, (2) to stabilize Mn2+-activated α5β1 integrins, and (3) to induce integrin-mediated FN fibril formation.
evidence: Inferred from AFM data, 9EG7 binding data, and FN fibril assembly data.

claim: 37% of TlnKo cells showed isotropic membrane protrusions (circumferential lamellipodia) upon Mn2+ treatment.
source: Upon Mn2+ treatment 37 ± 1% (n=684, mean ± standard deviation of three independent experiments) of the TlnKo cells showed isotropic membrane protrusions (circumferential lamellipodia) with small, dot-like aggregates of β1 integrin, kindlin-2, paxillin and ILK at the membrane periphery (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which eventually detached from the substrate leading to the collapse of the protruded membrane (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and live cell imaging in Video 1.

claim: Only 7% of KindKo cells established lamellipodia upon Mn2+ treatment.
source: In the case of KindKo cells, we analysed 652 cells in three independent experiments and found that only 7 ± 1% (mean ± standard deviation) of the cells established lamellipodia, which formed around the entire circumference in 2 ± 0.4% (mean ± standard deviation) of the cells.
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence images.

claim: Re-expression of Tln1V in TlnKo cells normalized FA formation and spreading on FN.
source: Importantly, re-expression of Tln1V in TlnKo cells or K2GFP in KindKo cells normalized FA formation and spreading on FN (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Re-expression of K2GFP in KindKo cells normalized FA formation and spreading on FN.
source: Importantly, re-expression of Tln1V in TlnKo cells or K2GFP in KindKo cells normalized FA formation and spreading on FN (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Kindlin-2 expressing TlnKo cells can initiate the formation of large lamellipodia and assemble β1 integrins in lamellipodial edges.
source: These findings indicate that kindlin-2 expressing TlnKo cells can initiate the formation of large lamellipodia and assemble β1 integrins in lamellipodial edges.
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence and dSTORM imaging data showing β1 integrin localization at lamellipodial edges in TlnKo cells.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of overexpressed GFP-tagged paxillin family members (paxillin, Hic-5 and leupaxin) in HEK-293 cells efficiently co-precipitated FLAG-tagged kindlin-2.
source: Immunoprecipitation of overexpressed green fluorescent protein (GFP)-tagged paxillin family members, paxillin, Hic-5 and leupaxin in HEK-293 cells with an anti-GFP antibody efficiently co-precipitated FLAG-tagged kindlin-2 (K2flag) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpressed GFP-tagged kindlin family members (kindlin-1, kindlin-2, kindlin-3) co-precipitated Cherry-paxillin.
source: Conversely, overexpressed GFP-tagged kindlin family members (kindlin-1, kindlin-2, kindlin-3) co-precipitated Cherry-paxillin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction between kindlin-2 and paxillin was dramatically reduced in the absence of the LIM1-4, LIM2-4 or LIM3-4 domains of paxillin.
source: Immunoprecipitations of GFP-tagged paxillin or kindlin-2 truncation mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A) revealed that the interaction between kindlin-2 and paxillin was dramatically reduced in the absence of the Lin-11, Isl-1 and Mec-3 (LIM)1-4, LIM2-4 or LIM3-4 domains of paxillin (Figure 4B), or the pleckstrin homology (PH) domain (K2ΔPHGFP; lacking amino acids 380-477) or the N-terminus of kindlin-2 including the F0, F1, and the N-terminal part of the F2 domains (K2NTGFP; terminating at the end of F1; spanning amino acids 1-229) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The interaction between kindlin-2 and paxillin was dramatically reduced in the absence of the PH domain of kindlin-2.
source: Immunoprecipitations of GFP-tagged paxillin or kindlin-2 truncation mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A) revealed that the interaction between kindlin-2 and paxillin was dramatically reduced in the absence of the Lin-11, Isl-1 and Mec-3 (LIM)1-4, LIM2-4 or LIM3-4 domains of paxillin (Figure 4B), or the pleckstrin homology (PH) domain (K2ΔPHGFP; lacking amino acids 380-477) or the N-terminus of kindlin-2 including the F0, F1, and the N-terminal part of the F2 domains (K2NTGFP; terminating at the end of F1; spanning amino acids 1-229) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of KindCtr lysates with antibodies against paxillin co-precipitated kindlin-2.
source: Importantly, immunoprecipitation of KindCtr lysates with antibodies against paxillin co-precipitated kindlin-2 (Figure 4D), confirming interactions between the endogenous proteins.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Binding of kindlin-2 to paxillin LIM3 domain and full-length paxillin is direct and Zn2+-dependent.
source: Pull down experiments with recombinant full-length paxillin or paxillin-LIM3 domain and recombinant kindlin-2 demonstrated that binding to LIM3 and full-length paxillin is direct, Zn2+-dependent and abrogated with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by recombinant protein pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Expression of K2GFP in KindKo cells rescued spreading and induced robust paxillin recruitment to β1 integrin-positive NAs.
source: KindKo cells were transduced with K2GFP or K2ΔPHGFP expression constructs, seeded on FN for different times and stained for β1 integrin, paxillin and F-actin. The experiments revealed that the expression of K2GFP in KindKo cells rescued spreading and induced robust paxillin recruitment to β1 integrin-positive NAs (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and fluorescence intensity line scans shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: Expression of K2ΔPHGFP failed to recruit paxillin to β1 integrin-positive adhesion sites at the rim of membrane protrusions.
source: In contrast, expression of K2ΔPHGFP failed to recruit paxillin to β1 integrin-positive adhesion sites at the rim of membrane protrusions (Figure 4F,G) and induce normal cell spreading (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A) despite proper, although weaker, localisation to β1 integrin-positive adhesion sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and fluorescence intensity line scans shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: Mature FAs in K2ΔPHGFP-expressing cells contained significant amounts of paxillin after 30 min.
source: Interestingly, mature FAs in K2ΔPHGFP-expressing cells were prominent after 30 min and contained significant amounts of paxillin, indicating that paxillin is recruited to mature FAs in a kindlin-2-independent manner (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Paxillin is recruited to mature FAs in a kindlin-2-independent manner.
source: Interestingly, mature FAs in K2ΔPHGFP-expressing cells were prominent after 30 min and contained significant amounts of paxillin, indicating that paxillin is recruited to mature FAs in a kindlin-2-independent manner (Figure 4F).
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence images showing paxillin in mature FAs of K2ΔPHGFP-expressing cells in Figure 4F.

claim: The PH domain of kindlin-2 directly binds the LIM3 domain of paxillin.
source: These findings indicate that the PH domain of kindlin-2 directly binds the LIM3 domain of paxillin and recruits paxillin into NAs but not into mature FAs.
evidence: Inferred from immunoprecipitation, pull-down, and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Kindlin-2 recruits paxillin into NAs but not into mature FAs.
source: These findings indicate that the PH domain of kindlin-2 directly binds the LIM3 domain of paxillin and recruits paxillin into NAs but not into mature FAs.
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence data showing paxillin recruitment to NAs in K2GFP-expressing cells but not K2ΔPHGFP-expressing cells, and paxillin presence in mature FAs of K2ΔPHGFP-expressing cells.

claim: EGF induced similar phosphorylation of tyrosine-992 (Y992) of the epidermal growth factor receptor (pY992-EGFR) in control, TlnKo and KindKo cells.
source: We found that EGF induced similar phosphorylation of tyrosine-992 (Y992) of the epidermal growth factor receptor (pY992-EGFR) in control, TlnKo and KindKo cells.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The phosphorylation of tyrosine-397 of FAK (pY379-FAK) in KindCtr cells was strongly induced after the adhesion of control cells on FN.
source: The phosphorylation of tyrosine-397 of FAK (pY379-FAK) in KindCtr cells was strongly induced after the adhesion of control cells on FN and was not further elevated after the addition of EGF and Mn2+ (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TlnKo cells increased pY397-FAK, pY31-Pxn and pY118-Pxn levels upon adhesion to FN, however, significantly less compared to control cells.
source: TlnKo cells also increased pY397-FAK as well as pY31-Pxn and pY118-Pxn levels upon adhesion to FN, however, significantly less compared to control cells (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: EGF and Mn2+ treatments further increased pY397-FAK levels in TlnKo cells and localized pY397-FAK to peripheral NA-like adhesions.
source: Furthermore, EGF and Mn2+ treatments further increased pY397-FAK levels in TlnKo cells and localized pY397-FAK to peripheral NA-like adhesions (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C, and immunofluorescence images in Figure 5B.

claim: KindKo cells seeded on FN or treated with EGF and Mn2+ failed to induce pY397-FAK, pY31-Pxn, pY118-Pxn.
source: In sharp contrast, KindKo cells seeded on FN or treated with EGF and Mn2+ failed to induce pY397-FAK, pY31-Pxn, pY118-Pxn (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C) and localize pY397-FAK to peripheral membrane regions (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: KindKo cells failed to localize pY397-FAK to peripheral membrane regions.
source: In sharp contrast, KindKo cells seeded on FN or treated with EGF and Mn2+ failed to induce pY397-FAK, pY31-Pxn, pY118-Pxn (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C) and localize pY397-FAK to peripheral membrane regions (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Re-expression of Talin1-Venus in TlnKo cells fully rescued FAK and paxillin signaling defects.
source: Importantly, re-expression of Talin1-Venus in TlnKo and Kindlin2-GFP and KindKo cells fully rescued these signaling defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Re-expression of Kindlin2-GFP in KindKo cells fully rescued FAK and paxillin signaling defects.
source: Importantly, re-expression of Talin1-Venus in TlnKo and Kindlin2-GFP and KindKo cells fully rescued these signaling defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Stable expression of K2GFP in KindKo cells rescued pY397-FAK and pS473-Akt levels.
source: Furthermore, stable expression of K2GFP in KindKo cells rescued pY397-FAK and pS473-Akt levels (Figure 5C) and co-precipitated paxillin and FAK with K2GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Stable expression of K2GFP in KindKo cells co-precipitated paxillin and FAK with K2GFP.
source: Furthermore, stable expression of K2GFP in KindKo cells rescued pY397-FAK and pS473-Akt levels (Figure 5C) and co-precipitated paxillin and FAK with K2GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stable expression of K2ΔPHGFP in KindKo cells failed to co-precipitate paxillin and FAK.
source: In contrast, stable expression of K2ΔPHGFP in KindKo cells failed to co-precipitate paxillin and FAK (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and induce pY397-FAK and pS473-Akt (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stable expression of K2ΔPHGFP in KindKo cells failed to induce pY397-FAK and pS473-Akt.
source: In contrast, stable expression of K2ΔPHGFP in KindKo cells failed to co-precipitate paxillin and FAK (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and induce pY397-FAK and pS473-Akt (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FN-seeded control and rescued cells showed Y410-p130Cas, pT308-Akt, S473-Akt and pT202/pY204 Erk1/2 phosphorylation after Mn2+ and/or EGF treatment.
source: In line with previous reports showing that the paxillin/FAK complex can trigger the activation of p130Cas (Zhang et al., 2014) and, in cooperation with EGFR signaling, the activation of Akt (Sulzmaier et al., 2014, Deakin et al., 2012), we observed Y410-p130Cas, pT308-Akt, S473-Akt and pT202/pY204 Erk1/2 phosphorylation after Mn2+ and/or EGF treatment of FN-seeded control and rescued cells, and to a slightly lesser extent TlnKo cells (Figure 5D, Figure 5— figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B, and citations to literature (Zhang et al., 2014; Sulzmaier et al., 2014; Deakin et al., 2012).

claim: FN-seeded KindKo cells failed to activate p130Cas and showed reduced Akt and Erk1/2 phosphorylation in response to EGF.
source: In contrast, FN-seeded KindKo cells failed to activate p130Cas and showed reduced Akt and Erk1/2 phosphorylation in response to EGF (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Inhibiting FAK reduced lamellipodia formation of TlnKo cells to an extent that was similar to untreated KindKo cells.
source: The experiments revealed that inhibiting FAK reduced lamellipodia formation of TlnKo cells to an extent that was similar to untreated KindKo cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by quantification of lamellipodia formation shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Overexpression of FAKGFP in KindKo cells resulted in high active FAK, increased lamellipodial formation and increased cell spreading.
source: Conversely, overexpression of FAKGFP in KindKo cells resulted in high active FAK, increased lamellipodial formation and increased cell spreading in TlnKo and KindKo cells (Figure 5F,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data, quantification of lamellipodia formation, and cell spreading area measurements shown in Figure 5F,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: The kindlin-2/paxillin complex in NAs recruits and activates FAK to induce cell spreading and increase the strength of Akt signaling.
source: Altogether, these findings show that the kindlin-2/paxillin complex in NAs recruits and activates FAK to induce cell spreading and increase the strength of Akt signaling.
evidence: Inferred from data showing kindlin-2/paxillin interaction, FAK activation, and cell spreading.

claim: Integrin affinity regulation (activation) is essential for fibroblast adhesion and depends on both talin and kindlin-2.
source: A major finding of our study demonstrates that integrin affinity regulation (activation) is essential for fibroblast adhesion and depends on both talin and kindlin-2 (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: Inferred from 9EG7 binding data, AFM measurements, and adhesion assays.

claim: The initial spreading of TlnKo and talin-depleted cells is short-lived.
source: The short-lived nature of the initial spreading of TlnKo and talin-depleted (Zhang et al., 2008) cells shows that talin concludes the integrin-mediated adhesion process in NAs (Figure 6F) and induces the maturation of FAs.
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data in Video 1 and citation to literature (Zhang et al., 2008).

claim: Talin concludes the integrin-mediated adhesion process in NAs and induces the maturation of FAs.
source: The short-lived nature of the initial spreading of TlnKo and talin-depleted (Zhang et al., 2008) cells shows that talin concludes the integrin-mediated adhesion process in NAs (Figure 6F) and induces the maturation of FAs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TlnKo cells form lamellipodia that collapse, and that talin re-expression rescues FA formation.
